Let function \(f\) be a quartic (4th-degree) polynomial shown below as a product of linear factors:

\[f(x)~=~(x+4)(x-9)(x-6)(x+8)\]

Find all the roots of polynomial \(f\). In other words, find all values of \(x\) such that \(f(x)=0\).

See the zero product property.

A polynomial equals zero whenever one of its factors equals zero.

Thus, the roots are -4 and 9 and 6 and -8.

Let function \(f\) be a quartic (4th-degree) polynomial shown below as a product of linear factors:

\[f(x)~=~(x+4)(x-2)(x-3)(x+5)\]

Find all the roots of polynomial \(f\). In other words, find all values of \(x\) such that \(f(x)=0\).

See the zero product property.

A polynomial equals zero whenever one of its factors equals zero.

Thus, the roots are -4 and 2 and 3 and -5.

Let function \(f\) be a quartic (4th-degree) polynomial shown below as a product of linear factors:

\[f(x)~=~(x-5)(x-2)(x-4)(x+3)\]

Find all the roots of polynomial \(f\). In other words, find all values of \(x\) such that \(f(x)=0\).

Let function \(f\) be a quartic (4th-degree) polynomial shown below as a product of linear factors:

\[f(x)~=~(x-9)(x-7)(x-5)(x-8)\]

Find all the roots of polynomial \(f\). In other words, find all values of \(x\) such that \(f(x)=0\).

See the zero product property.

A polynomial equals zero whenever one of its factors equals zero.

Thus, the roots are 9 and 7 and 5 and 8.

A polynomial is sketched below.


Which polynomial (in factored form) best matches the sketch?

If a polynomial has a factor of \(x-r\), then there will be an \(x\)-intercept at point \((r,0)\).

In this case, the roots (the \(x\)-intercepts) are at:

\[-4,\,-2\]

Thus, the factors are \(x+4\) and \(x+2\). Notice, the \(x\)-intercepts where the curve "bounces" off the \(x\) axis correspond to an even multiplicity, in this case a multiplicity of 2. So, we know the curve could be represented by the function below:

\[y=a(x+4)(x+2)^2\]

where \(a\) is some constant.

Lastly, we need to determine whether \(a\) should be positive or negative. In this problem, either \(a=1\) or \(a=-1\). To determine this, look at the right side of the graph. Specifically, we are considering the end behavior of polynomials. Notice that once \(x\) is larger than \(-2\), all the factors will be positive, so only \(a\) will dictate whether the function on the right side is positive or negative.


Notice, on the right side, the function is heading down. I guess more importantly, as \(x\to \infty\) we see the function is negative. This implies that \(a\) is negative. So, in this case, \(a=-1\).

\[y=-(x+4)(x+2)^2\]

A polynomial is sketched below.


Which polynomial (in factored form) best matches the sketch?

If a polynomial has a factor of \(x-r\), then there will be an \(x\)-intercept at point \((r,0)\).

In this case, the roots (the \(x\)-intercepts) are at:

\[-2,\,1,\,3\]

Thus, the factors are \(x+2\) and \(x-1\) and \(x-3\). Notice, the \(x\)-intercepts where the curve "bounces" off the \(x\) axis correspond to an even multiplicity, in this case a multiplicity of 2. So, we know the curve could be represented by the function below:

\[y=a(x+2)(x-1)^2(x-3)\]

where \(a\) is some constant.

Lastly, we need to determine whether \(a\) should be positive or negative. In this problem, either \(a=1\) or \(a=-1\). To determine this, look at the right side of the graph. Specifically, we are considering the end behavior of polynomials. Notice that once \(x\) is larger than \(3\), all the factors will be positive, so only \(a\) will dictate whether the function on the right side is positive or negative.


Notice, on the right side, the function is heading down. I guess more importantly, as \(x\to \infty\) we see the function is negative. This implies that \(a\) is negative. So, in this case, \(a=-1\).

\[y=-(x+2)(x-1)^2(x-3)\]

And then, since multiplication is commutative, the factors can be written in any order. In this case, the correct answer is:

\[y=-(x-1)^2(x-3)(x+2)\]

In this case, the roots (the \(x\)-intercepts) are at:

\[2,\,8\]

Thus, the factors are \(x-2\) and \(x-8\). Notice, the \(x\)-intercepts where the curve "bounces" off the \(x\) axis correspond to an even multiplicity, in this case a multiplicity of 2. So, we know the curve could be represented by the function below:

\[y=a(x-2)(x-8)^2\]

where \(a\) is some constant.

Lastly, we need to determine whether \(a\) should be positive or negative. In this problem, either \(a=1\) or \(a=-1\). To determine this, look at the right side of the graph. Specifically, we are considering the end behavior of polynomials. Notice that once \(x\) is larger than \(8\), all the factors will be positive, so only \(a\) will dictate whether the function on the right side is positive or negative.


Notice, on the right side, the function is heading up. I guess more importantly, as \(x\to \infty\) we see the function is positive. This implies that \(a\) is positive. So, in this case, \(a=1\).

\[y=(x-2)(x-8)^2\]

And then, since multiplication is commutative, the factors can be written in any order. In this case, the correct answer is:

\[y=(x-8)^2(x-2)\]

Let function \(f\) be a polynomial with real coefficients. If \(f(6+9i)=0\), then that implies that \(6+9i\) is one root of the polynomial.

What is the other known root?

When a polynomial with real coefficients has a complex root, we know the complex conjugate is also a root.

So, the answer is 6-9i

So, the answer is -9+2i

Let \(f\) represent a quartic (4th degree) polynomial with integer coefficients.

\[f(x)~=~{3}x^{4}+{28}x^{3}+{324}x^{2}+{396}x+{97}\]

One of the roots is \(-4+9i\), where \(i=\sqrt{-1}\).

\[f(-4+9i)~=~0\]

This quartic polynomial has at least 1 rational root. Find all the rational roots.

We know that complex roots show up as complex-conjugate pairs. So, since \(-4+9i\) is a root, we also know \(-4-9i\) is another root. This accounts for two roots.

The fundamental theorem of algebra promises "every non-zero, single-variable, degree n polynomial with complex coefficients has, counted with multiplicity, exactly n complex roots."

So, we know there will be a total of 4 roots.

Thus, we should be able to express \(f(x)\) in a semi-factored form (with yet to be determined coefficients \(a\) and \(b\) and \(c\)).

\[f(x)~=~(ax^2+bx+c)(x-(-4+9i))(x-(-4-9i))\]

Distribute the negatives across the inner parentheses.

\[f(x)~=~(ax^2+bx+c)(x+4-9i)(x+4+9i)\]

Now use a box to multiply the two complex factors.


Remember, \(i^2=-1\), so \(-81i^2=81\). Combine like terms.

\[f(x)~=~(ax^2+bx+c)(x^2+8x+97)\]

Now... we know this semi-factored form and the standard form are equivalent expressions.

\[(ax^2+bx+c)(x^2+8x+97)~\equiv~{3}x^{4}+{28}x^{3}+{324}x^{2}+{396}x+{97}\]

So, we can divide both sides by \(x^{2}+{8}x+{97}\).

\[ax^2+bx+c~=~\frac{{3}x^{4}+{28}x^{3}+{324}x^{2}+{396}x+{97}}{x^{2}+{8}x+{97}}\]

Use the box method to divide.


So,

\[f(x)~=~({3}x^{2}+{4}x+{1})(x^{2}+{8}x+{97})\]

We have expressed the quartic polynomial as the product of two quadratic polynomials. Remember, our goal is to find solutions to \(f(x)=0\). We already know that \(x=-4+9i\) and \(x=-4-9i\) are solutions, and those two roots correspond to the factor \(x^{2}+{8}x+{97}\) equaling 0. By setting the other quadratic factor, \({3}x^{2}+{4}x+{1}\), equal to zero, we can find the other roots.

\[{3}x^{2}+{4}x+{1}=0\]

Use the quadratic formula: if \(ax^2+bx+c=0\) then \(x=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}\).

\[x=\frac{-(4)\pm\sqrt{(4)^2-4(3)(1)}}{2(3)}\]

Simplify.

\[x=\frac{-4\pm\sqrt{16-12}}{6}\]

Simplify.

\[x=\frac{-4\pm\sqrt{4}}{6}\]

Simplify.

\[x=\frac{-4\pm2}{6}\]

Split into two different fraction.

\[\begin{align} x&=\frac{-4+2}{6} &&& x&=\frac{-4-2}{6} \\\\ x&=\frac{-2}{6} &&& x&=\frac{-6}{6} \\\\ x&=\frac{-1}{3} &&& x&=-1 \end{align}\]

Now we know all four roots. We could express \(f\) in fully factored form.

\[f(x)~=~({3}x+{1})(x+{1})(x-(-4+9i))(x-(-4-9i))\]

Or, if you are not into complex factors, you could also express \(f\) as factored as possible with integer coefficients.

\[f(x)~=~({3}x+{1})(x+{1})(x^{2}+{8}x+{97})\]

Anyway, the two rational roots are \(\frac{-1}{3}\) and \(-1\).

Let \(f\) represent a quartic (4th degree) polynomial with integer coefficients.

\[f(x)~=~{3}x^{4}-{16}x^{3}+{78}x^{2}-{184}x+{119}\]

One of the roots is \(1+4i\), where \(i=\sqrt{-1}\).

\[f(1+4i)~=~0\]

This quartic polynomial has at least 1 rational root. Find all the rational roots.

We know that complex roots show up as complex-conjugate pairs. So, since \(1+4i\) is a root, we also know \(1-4i\) is another root. This accounts for two roots.

The fundamental theorem of algebra promises "every non-zero, single-variable, degree n polynomial with complex coefficients has, counted with multiplicity, exactly n complex roots."

So, we know there will be a total of 4 roots.

Thus, we should be able to express \(f(x)\) in a semi-factored form (with yet to be determined coefficients \(a\) and \(b\) and \(c\)).

\[f(x)~=~(ax^2+bx+c)(x-(1+4i))(x-(1-4i))\]

Distribute the negatives across the inner parentheses.

\[f(x)~=~(ax^2+bx+c)(x-1-4i)(x-1+4i)\]

Now use a box to multiply the two complex factors.


Remember, \(i^2=-1\), so \(-16i^2=16\). Combine like terms.

\[f(x)~=~(ax^2+bx+c)(x^2-2x+17)\]

Now... we know this semi-factored form and the standard form are equivalent expressions.

\[(ax^2+bx+c)(x^2-2x+17)~\equiv~{3}x^{4}-{16}x^{3}+{78}x^{2}-{184}x+{119}\]

So, we can divide both sides by \(x^{2}-{2}x+{17}\).

\[ax^2+bx+c~=~\frac{{3}x^{4}-{16}x^{3}+{78}x^{2}-{184}x+{119}}{x^{2}-{2}x+{17}}\]

Use the box method to divide.


So,

\[f(x)~=~({3}x^{2}-{10}x+{7})(x^{2}-{2}x+{17})\]

We have expressed the quartic polynomial as the product of two quadratic polynomials. Remember, our goal is to find solutions to \(f(x)=0\). We already know that \(x=1+4i\) and \(x=1-4i\) are solutions, and those two roots correspond to the factor \(x^{2}-{2}x+{17}\) equaling 0. By setting the other quadratic factor, \({3}x^{2}-{10}x+{7}\), equal to zero, we can find the other roots.

\[{3}x^{2}-{10}x+{7}=0\]

Use the quadratic formula: if \(ax^2+bx+c=0\) then \(x=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}\).

\[x=\frac{-(-10)\pm\sqrt{(-10)^2-4(3)(7)}}{2(3)}\]

Simplify.

\[x=\frac{10\pm\sqrt{100-84}}{6}\]

Simplify.

\[x=\frac{10\pm\sqrt{16}}{6}\]

Simplify.

\[x=\frac{10\pm4}{6}\]

Split into two different fraction.

\[\begin{align} x&=\frac{10+4}{6} &&& x&=\frac{10-4}{6} \\\\ x&=\frac{14}{6} &&& x&=\frac{6}{6} \\\\ x&=\frac{7}{3} &&& x&=1 \end{align}\]

Now we know all four roots. We could express \(f\) in fully factored form.

\[f(x)~=~(x-{1})({3}x-{7})(x-(1+4i))(x-(1-4i))\]

Or, if you are not into complex factors, you could also express \(f\) as factored as possible with integer coefficients.

\[f(x)~=~(x-{1})({3}x-{7})(x^{2}-{2}x+{17})\]

Anyway, the two rational roots are \(1\) and \(\frac{7}{3}\).

Let \(f\) represent a quartic (4th degree) polynomial with integer coefficients.

\[f(x)~=~{7}x^{4}-{81}x^{3}+{286}x^{2}-{226}x-{156}\]

One of the roots is \(5-i\), where \(i=\sqrt{-1}\).

\[f(5-i)~=~0\]

This quartic polynomial has at least 1 rational root. Find all the rational roots.

We know that complex roots show up as complex-conjugate pairs. So, since \(5-i\) is a root, we also know \(5+i\) is another root. This accounts for two roots.

The fundamental theorem of algebra promises "every non-zero, single-variable, degree n polynomial with complex coefficients has, counted with multiplicity, exactly n complex roots."

So, we know there will be a total of 4 roots.

Thus, we should be able to express \(f(x)\) in a semi-factored form (with yet to be determined coefficients \(a\) and \(b\) and \(c\)).

\[f(x)~=~(ax^2+bx+c)(x-(5-i))(x-(5+i))\]

Distribute the negatives across the inner parentheses.

\[f(x)~=~(ax^2+bx+c)(x-5+i)(x-5-i)\]

Now use a box to multiply the two complex factors.


Remember, \(i^2=-1\), so \(-1i^2=1\). Combine like terms.

\[f(x)~=~(ax^2+bx+c)(x^2-10x+26)\]

Now... we know this semi-factored form and the standard form are equivalent expressions.

\[(ax^2+bx+c)(x^2-10x+26)~\equiv~{7}x^{4}-{81}x^{3}+{286}x^{2}-{226}x-{156}\]

So, we can divide both sides by \(x^{2}-{10}x+{26}\).

\[ax^2+bx+c~=~\frac{{7}x^{4}-{81}x^{3}+{286}x^{2}-{226}x-{156}}{x^{2}-{10}x+{26}}\]

Use the box method to divide.


So,

\[f(x)~=~({7}x^{2}-{11}x-{6})(x^{2}-{10}x+{26})\]

We have expressed the quartic polynomial as the product of two quadratic polynomials. Remember, our goal is to find solutions to \(f(x)=0\). We already know that \(x=5-i\) and \(x=5+i\) are solutions, and those two roots correspond to the factor \(x^{2}-{10}x+{26}\) equaling 0. By setting the other quadratic factor, \({7}x^{2}-{11}x-{6}\), equal to zero, we can find the other roots.

\[{7}x^{2}-{11}x-{6}=0\]

Use the quadratic formula: if \(ax^2+bx+c=0\) then \(x=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}\).

\[x=\frac{-(-11)\pm\sqrt{(-11)^2-4(7)(-6)}}{2(7)}\]

Simplify.

\[x=\frac{11\pm\sqrt{121+168}}{14}\]

Simplify.

\[x=\frac{11\pm\sqrt{289}}{14}\]

Simplify.

\[x=\frac{11\pm17}{14}\]

Split into two different fraction.

\[\begin{align} x&=\frac{11+17}{14} &&& x&=\frac{11-17}{14} \\\\ x&=\frac{28}{14} &&& x&=\frac{-6}{14} \\\\ x&=2 &&& x&=\frac{-3}{7} \end{align}\]

Now we know all four roots. We could express \(f\) in fully factored form.

\[f(x)~=~({7}x+{3})(x-{2})(x-(5-i))(x-(5+i))\]

Or, if you are not into complex factors, you could also express \(f\) as factored as possible with integer coefficients.

\[f(x)~=~({7}x+{3})(x-{2})(x^{2}-{10}x+{26})\]

Anyway, the two rational roots are \(\frac{-3}{7}\) and \(2\).

Let \(f\) represent a quartic (4th degree) polynomial with integer coefficients.

\[f(x)~=~{15}x^{4}+{49}x^{3}+{180}x^{2}+{174}x-{80}\]

One of the roots is \(-1-3i\), where \(i=\sqrt{-1}\).

\[f(-1-3i)~=~0\]

This quartic polynomial has at least 1 rational root. Find all the rational roots.

We know that complex roots show up as complex-conjugate pairs. So, since \(-1-3i\) is a root, we also know \(-1+3i\) is another root. This accounts for two roots.

The fundamental theorem of algebra promises "every non-zero, single-variable, degree n polynomial with complex coefficients has, counted with multiplicity, exactly n complex roots."

So, we know there will be a total of 4 roots.

Thus, we should be able to express \(f(x)\) in a semi-factored form (with yet to be determined coefficients \(a\) and \(b\) and \(c\)).

\[f(x)~=~(ax^2+bx+c)(x-(-1-3i))(x-(-1+3i))\]

Distribute the negatives across the inner parentheses.

\[f(x)~=~(ax^2+bx+c)(x+1+3i)(x+1-3i)\]

Now use a box to multiply the two complex factors.


Remember, \(i^2=-1\), so \(-9i^2=9\). Combine like terms.

\[f(x)~=~(ax^2+bx+c)(x^2+2x+10)\]

Now... we know this semi-factored form and the standard form are equivalent expressions.

\[(ax^2+bx+c)(x^2+2x+10)~\equiv~{15}x^{4}+{49}x^{3}+{180}x^{2}+{174}x-{80}\]

So, we can divide both sides by \(x^{2}+{2}x+{10}\).

\[ax^2+bx+c~=~\frac{{15}x^{4}+{49}x^{3}+{180}x^{2}+{174}x-{80}}{x^{2}+{2}x+{10}}\]

Use the box method to divide.


So,

\[f(x)~=~({15}x^{2}+{19}x-{8})(x^{2}+{2}x+{10})\]

We have expressed the quartic polynomial as the product of two quadratic polynomials. Remember, our goal is to find solutions to \(f(x)=0\). We already know that \(x=-1-3i\) and \(x=-1+3i\) are solutions, and those two roots correspond to the factor \(x^{2}+{2}x+{10}\) equaling 0. By setting the other quadratic factor, \({15}x^{2}+{19}x-{8}\), equal to zero, we can find the other roots.

\[{15}x^{2}+{19}x-{8}=0\]

Use the quadratic formula: if \(ax^2+bx+c=0\) then \(x=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}\).

\[x=\frac{-(19)\pm\sqrt{(19)^2-4(15)(-8)}}{2(15)}\]

Simplify.

\[x=\frac{-19\pm\sqrt{361+480}}{30}\]

Simplify.

\[x=\frac{-19\pm\sqrt{841}}{30}\]

Simplify.

\[x=\frac{-19\pm29}{30}\]

Split into two different fraction.

\[\begin{align} x&=\frac{-19+29}{30} &&& x&=\frac{-19-29}{30} \\\\ x&=\frac{10}{30} &&& x&=\frac{-48}{30} \\\\ x&=\frac{1}{3} &&& x&=\frac{-8}{5} \end{align}\]

Now we know all four roots. We could express \(f\) in fully factored form.

\[f(x)~=~({3}x-{1})({5}x+{8})(x-(-1-3i))(x-(-1+3i))\]

Or, if you are not into complex factors, you could also express \(f\) as factored as possible with integer coefficients.

\[f(x)~=~({3}x-{1})({5}x+{8})(x^{2}+{2}x+{10})\]

Anyway, the two rational roots are \(\frac{1}{3}\) and \(\frac{-8}{5}\).

\[f(-1-4i)~=~0\]

This quartic polynomial has at least 1 rational root. Find all the rational roots.

We know that complex roots show up as complex-conjugate pairs. So, since \(-1-4i\) is a root, we also know \(-1+4i\) is another root. This accounts for two roots.

The fundamental theorem of algebra promises "every non-zero, single-variable, degree n polynomial with complex coefficients has, counted with multiplicity, exactly n complex roots."

So, we know there will be a total of 4 roots.

Thus, we should be able to express \(f(x)\) in a semi-factored form (with yet to be determined coefficients \(a\) and \(b\) and \(c\)).

\[f(x)~=~(ax^2+bx+c)(x-(-1-4i))(x-(-1+4i))\]

Distribute the negatives across the inner parentheses.

\[f(x)~=~(ax^2+bx+c)(x+1+4i)(x+1-4i)\]

Now use a box to multiply the two complex factors.


Remember, \(i^2=-1\), so \(-16i^2=16\). Combine like terms.

\[f(x)~=~(ax^2+bx+c)(x^2+2x+17)\]

Now... we know this semi-factored form and the standard form are equivalent expressions.

\[(ax^2+bx+c)(x^2+2x+17)~\equiv~{8}x^{4}+{6}x^{3}+{109}x^{2}-{184}x-{119}\]

So, we can divide both sides by \(x^{2}+{2}x+{17}\).

\[ax^2+bx+c~=~\frac{{8}x^{4}+{6}x^{3}+{109}x^{2}-{184}x-{119}}{x^{2}+{2}x+{17}}\]

Use the box method to divide.


So,

\[f(x)~=~({8}x^{2}-{10}x-{7})(x^{2}+{2}x+{17})\]

We have expressed the quartic polynomial as the product of two quadratic polynomials. Remember, our goal is to find solutions to \(f(x)=0\). We already know that \(x=-1-4i\) and \(x=-1+4i\) are solutions, and those two roots correspond to the factor \(x^{2}+{2}x+{17}\) equaling 0. By setting the other quadratic factor, \({8}x^{2}-{10}x-{7}\), equal to zero, we can find the other roots.

\[{8}x^{2}-{10}x-{7}=0\]

Use the quadratic formula: if \(ax^2+bx+c=0\) then \(x=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}\).

\[x=\frac{-(-10)\pm\sqrt{(-10)^2-4(8)(-7)}}{2(8)}\]

Simplify.

\[x=\frac{10\pm\sqrt{100+224}}{16}\]

Simplify.

\[x=\frac{10\pm\sqrt{324}}{16}\]

Simplify.

\[x=\frac{10\pm18}{16}\]

Split into two different fraction.

\[\begin{align} x&=\frac{10+18}{16} &&& x&=\frac{10-18}{16} \\\\ x&=\frac{28}{16} &&& x&=\frac{-8}{16} \\\\ x&=\frac{7}{4} &&& x&=\frac{-1}{2} \end{align}\]

Now we know all four roots. We could express \(f\) in fully factored form.

\[f(x)~=~({4}x-{7})({2}x+{1})(x-(-1-4i))(x-(-1+4i))\]

Or, if you are not into complex factors, you could also express \(f\) as factored as possible with integer coefficients.

\[f(x)~=~({4}x-{7})({2}x+{1})(x^{2}+{2}x+{17})\]

Anyway, the two rational roots are \(\frac{7}{4}\) and \(\frac{-1}{2}\).

Let \(f\) represent a quartic (4th degree) polynomial with integer coefficients.

\[f(x)~=~{56}x^{4}+{79}x^{3}+{200}x^{2}-{193}x-{70}\]

One of the roots is \(-1-2i\), where \(i=\sqrt{-1}\).

\[f(-1-2i)~=~0\]

This quartic polynomial has at least 1 rational root. Find all the rational roots.

We know that complex roots show up as complex-conjugate pairs. So, since \(-1-2i\) is a root, we also know \(-1+2i\) is another root. This accounts for two roots.

The fundamental theorem of algebra promises "every non-zero, single-variable, degree n polynomial with complex coefficients has, counted with multiplicity, exactly n complex roots."

So, we know there will be a total of 4 roots.

Thus, we should be able to express \(f(x)\) in a semi-factored form (with yet to be determined coefficients \(a\) and \(b\) and \(c\)).

\[f(x)~=~(ax^2+bx+c)(x-(-1-2i))(x-(-1+2i))\]

Distribute the negatives across the inner parentheses.

\[f(x)~=~(ax^2+bx+c)(x+1+2i)(x+1-2i)\]

Now use a box to multiply the two complex factors.


Remember, \(i^2=-1\), so \(-4i^2=4\). Combine like terms.

\[f(x)~=~(ax^2+bx+c)(x^2+2x+5)\]

Now... we know this semi-factored form and the standard form are equivalent expressions.

\[(ax^2+bx+c)(x^2+2x+5)~\equiv~{56}x^{4}+{79}x^{3}+{200}x^{2}-{193}x-{70}\]

So, we can divide both sides by \(x^{2}+{2}x+{5}\).

\[ax^2+bx+c~=~\frac{{56}x^{4}+{79}x^{3}+{200}x^{2}-{193}x-{70}}{x^{2}+{2}x+{5}}\]

Use the box method to divide.


So,

\[f(x)~=~({56}x^{2}-{33}x-{14})(x^{2}+{2}x+{5})\]

We have expressed the quartic polynomial as the product of two quadratic polynomials. Remember, our goal is to find solutions to \(f(x)=0\). We already know that \(x=-1-2i\) and \(x=-1+2i\) are solutions, and those two roots correspond to the factor \(x^{2}+{2}x+{5}\) equaling 0. By setting the other quadratic factor, \({56}x^{2}-{33}x-{14}\), equal to zero, we can find the other roots.

\[{56}x^{2}-{33}x-{14}=0\]

Use the quadratic formula: if \(ax^2+bx+c=0\) then \(x=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}\).

\[x=\frac{-(-33)\pm\sqrt{(-33)^2-4(56)(-14)}}{2(56)}\]

Simplify.

\[x=\frac{33\pm\sqrt{1089+3136}}{112}\]

Simplify.

\[x=\frac{33\pm\sqrt{4225}}{112}\]

Simplify.

\[x=\frac{33\pm65}{112}\]

Split into two different fraction.

\[\begin{align} x&=\frac{33+65}{112} &&& x&=\frac{33-65}{112} \\\\ x&=\frac{98}{112} &&& x&=\frac{-32}{112} \\\\ x&=\frac{7}{8} &&& x&=\frac{-2}{7} \end{align}\]

Now we know all four roots. We could express \(f\) in fully factored form.

\[f(x)~=~({8}x-{7})({7}x+{2})(x-(-1-2i))(x-(-1+2i))\]
